cross_product_finding: Private endpoints (and VPC peering) are network-boundary access-control primitives - they answer 'which network can even reach the cluster', a question that server/'s RBAC privilege model never has to answer since server/ docs assume the caller already has network access to the cluster. Combined with the findings on the other security/ pages in this batch, the overall picture for Capella access control is at least four distinct, non-overlapping layers found across this batch's pages: (1) network boundary - private endpoints, VPC peering, allowed IPs, restrict public access (this page + security.json); (2) transport/identity authentication - TLS (always-on), root certificates, X.509 client certs, SSO/MFA (security-certificates.json + security.json); (3) authorization - organization/project user roles, cluster credentials (security.json); (4) operational governance - auditing, gated by a support/service plan rather than by privilege or edition (auditing.json + audit-management.json). None of these four layers is well-served by shoehorning it into requiresPrivilege, which was designed for server/'s single flat list of named RBAC privileges (e.g. privilege:query-manage-index). This strongly supports the coordinator treating Capella's security/ vocabulary as its own sub-ontology with cross-links to server/ only where content is explicitly deferred to server/ docs (as seen with the audit event reference in auditing.json), rather than trying to retrofit it onto the requiresPrivilege/requiresEdition/availableSince predicates built for server/.
